questions.label: 1. Farm boundaries physically walked and GPS polygon captured — Ask Violet to provide GPS locations and trace these along farm boundaries with phone maps. Hopefully, the Violet team can do this with you monitoring
2. CAR number verified on-site against car.gov.br printout — Violet to provide in advance/ check against car.gov.br
3. CAR polygon overlaid on satellite image — no inconsistency with actual farm boundary — Same as farm boundaries. Violet can provide and walk you through
4. Reserva Legal area identified and physically inspected — vegetation status noted — To ask farmers to show you the legal reserve area to ensure preservation, no encroachment etc.
5. APP / riparian buffer strips present and vegetated along all watercourses — Same as above
6. No evidence of recent deforestation (fresh stumps, burn scars, bare soil clearing) — General inspection across farm, in particular around boundaries, legal reserve, and APP zones
7. No active deforestation observed during visit — Same as above
8. No IBAMA embargo or environmental infraction notice visible on farm — Lookout for any signs or notices
9. Farm not within or adjacent to a Conservation Unit (verified GIS overlay) — Check with Violet if available map data for conservation areas and indigenous lands
10. Farm not overlapping with Indigenous Land or Quilombola territory (verified GIS)
11. Presence of native shade trees in cocoa plots (agroforestry / cabruca system) — Check tree species
12. Soil erosion or degradation — note severity and location if present — Check for exposed tree roots, small channels, soil build-up around fences
13. Water bodies (rivers, streams, ponds) condition — sedimentation, colour, odour assessed — Check for clarity, eutrophication (algal bloom at surface)
14. Evidence of burning (charcoal, ash, scorched vegetation) on property — note if found — Check for charcoal, ash, scorched vegetation
15. Children observed on farm — ages estimated and activity noted — Ask for ages of chlidren on farm. Note if any serious suspicions of age significantly lower than stated.
16. NO children observed in cocoa harvest, handling chemicals, or using bladed tools
17. All workers on site appear to be adults (18+)
18. Workers observed using PPE during pesticide application or handling
19. Worker welfare: toilet facilities, clean drinking water, shaded rest area visible
20. No workers observed in apparent distress, under coercion, or physically restrained
23. Agrochemical store located and position relative to water sources and dwellings noted — How close are chemicals stored compared to water sources and housing/ worker accomodation?
24. Store is locked, ventilated, and built of non-absorbent materials
25. All products in original labelled containers — no unlabelled or decanted products
26. No MAPA-prohibited products present (record any prohibited products found by name) — Note all product names to be checked later.
27. No WHO Class Ia or Ib products observed (record any found by name and active ingredient)
29. Full PPE kit present — gloves, boots, overalls, mask, goggles — condition assessed
30. Empty containers: triple-rinsed, punctured, stored for inpEV / campo limpo collection
31. No empty containers burned, buried, or left in fields or near water sources
32. Spray equipment in good condition — no visible leaks or damage
34. Cocoa tree condition assessed — estimated age, variety, disease pressure (witches' broom, black pod)
35. Shade canopy cover estimated (%) — adequate density for climate resilience
37. Harvest infrastructure: fermentation boxes, drying facilities — hygiene and condition assessed
38. Cocoa storage — moisture protection, pest/rodent control, stored separately from chemicals
39. Traceability: weighing records, delivery receipts, cooperative sale documentation present
40. Farm records / farmer notebook maintained (inputs, yields, sales)
41. Certification signage or documentation (RA, Fairtrade, organic) present if claimed
42. CAR registration certificate or SICAR printout
43. Land title / escritura / CCIR / INCRA título (whichever applies to this farm)
44. Loan contract — cover page, key terms page, and signature page
45. Agronomic prescriptions (receitas agronômicas) for all pesticides in use
47. Certification audit report / certificate (Rainforest Alliance, Fairtrade, organic) if held
48. Environmental infraction notices or IBAMA embargoes (if any exist)
49. Worker employment contracts / fichas de registro (if hired labour is used)
50. GPS polygon map of farm (field-captured or CAR polygon printout)
51. Photograph of farm entrance with GPS geotag
52. Photograph of Reserva Legal area vegetation
54. Photograph of cocoa stand showing variety and condition
55. Photograph of fermentation boxes and / or drying facilities
Q1. How long have you been working as a field extension agent for Kawa? What was your role before this? — Assess experience level and continuity.
Q2. How many farmers are currently in your caseload? How many farm visits do you typically complete per month? — Benchmark: minimum 2 visits/farmer/season. Flag if >150 farmers per agent.
Q3. What formal training or qualifications do you have in agronomy, agriculture, or a related field? — Ask to see certificates or training records. Note any gaps in ESG-related training.

Q4. What ESG or sustainability training have you received from Kawa or an external provider? When was the most recent training? — Look for training on: child labour, deforestation, chemical safety, gender, grievances.

Q5. Do you have a written job description that includes ESG responsibilities? Are ESG KPIs included in your performance review? — Absence of ESG KPIs is a governance gap. Ask to see the job description.

Q6. Can you describe what 'child labour' and 'worst forms of child labour' mean under Brazilian law (ECA) and ILO Convention 182? — Test knowledge: minimum age 14; hazardous work prohibited under 18. Flag inability to define.
Q7. Have you ever observed or suspected child labour on a farm in your caseload? What did you do? — Listen for: immediate reporting, documentation, follow-up visit, referral to social services.

Q8. Does Kawa have a written child labour policy and a clear escalation procedure? Have you read it? Can you describe the steps? — Ask for the policy document reference. Inability to describe steps = procedural gap.
Q9. How do you verify that school-age children in farmer households are attending school regularly? — Best practice: confirm school enrolment record or directly with school. Note any proxy methods.
Q10. Do you ask farmers directly about children working on the farm during your visits? What questions do you ask? — Assess whether questioning is routine and specific, or superficial.
Q11. Are you aware of community or government resources (CRAS, Conselho Tutelar) available to refer child labour cases? — Knowledge of local referral pathways is essential for effective safeguarding.

Q12. How do you monitor for deforestation or land clearing among your farmers? What tools or systems does Kawa provide? — Best practice: satellite monitoring (PRODES/DETER alerts), farm polygon mapping, field observation.

Q13. Do you verify each farmer's CAR registration during your visits? How do you check the status and accuracy of the CAR? — Should be checking car.gov.br or SICAR. Note whether this is routine or ad hoc.
Q14. Do you check whether any farmers' farms overlap with Conservation Units, Indigenous Lands, or IBAMA embargoes? — Best practice: GIS overlay check using FUNAI/ICMBio/IBAMA datasets.

Q15. Have any farmers in your caseload received an IBAMA infraction notice or been under embargo for deforestation? What happened? — Listen for: exclusion from programme, remediation plan, continued support with conditions.

Q16. Does Kawa have a deforestation cut-off date (e.g. post-2020 = exclusion)? Are you clear on what to do if a polygon shows post-cut-off deforestation? — EUDR cut-off is 31 December 2020. Clarity on this is critical.

Q17. Are you familiar with the EUDR and its implications for your farmers' cocoa supply chain? Have you received specific training? — EUDR is a significant regulatory risk for Brazilian cocoa exports to EU markets.
Q18. When you visit a farm, do you inspect the agrochemical storage area? What do you look for? — Should check: locked, ventilated, labelled containers, no prohibited products, no children's access.

Q20. Are you aware of any prohibited or highly hazardous pesticides (WHO Class Ia/Ib or MAPA lista proibida)? Can you name examples? — Test knowledge. Should know: endosulfan banned; paraquat restricted; copper products require care.
Q21. How do you advise farmers on PPE use? Do you check PPE condition and availability during visits? — Best practice: physical inspection of PPE; demonstration of correct use; replacement records.

Q22. Does Kawa provide agrochemical alternatives, integrated pest management (IPM) training, or support for reducing chemical inputs? — Positive indicator of proactive risk management and sustainability transition support.
Q23. How do you handle a situation where a farmer is using a product you know to be harmful or prohibited? — Listen for: immediate advice, documentation, escalation to Kawa agronomist, follow-up.
Q24. What is your role in the loan onboarding process for farmers? Do you participate in explaining loan terms? — Assess whether agents understand their responsibility for informed consent quality.
Q25. How do you verify that a farmer has genuinely understood the loan terms before signing? — Best practice: farmer repeats terms back; independent verification; translated contract.
Q26. Do you conduct a basic repayment capacity assessment before recommending a farmer for a loan? — Should consider: income, existing debt, household size, seasonal income volatility.
Q27. Have you ever felt pressure from Kawa management or been given targets to sign up farmers quickly? — Sensitive but critical. Note tone and candour of response.

Q28. How are community guarantee / solidarity group arrangements explained to farmers? Do you facilitate group formation? — Check whether agent explains cross-liability clearly and that group formation is voluntary.
Q29. Do you follow up with farmers after loan disbursement to check they understand repayments and are managing well? — Post-disbursement follow-up is a good practice indicator for client protection.
Q30. Are farmers in your caseload aware that they can raise complaints about Kawa? How do they know? — Best practice: grievance mechanism communicated proactively at onboarding.
Q31. Have any farmers raised complaints? About what? How were they resolved? — Listen for: range of issues, response time, farmer satisfaction, systemic issues.
Q32. Have you ever had a complaint raised against you personally? How was it handled? — Tests whether internal accountability mechanisms exist and function.
Q33. Do you actively seek out women farmers in your caseload for extension visits and training? — Women are often underserved by extension systems. Note structural barriers.
Q34. Do you adapt your advisory approach for female-headed households? — Gender-responsive extension is a positive indicator.

Q35. Are there indigenous or quilombola communities in your area? Have you received training on FPIC or indigenous rights? — Relevant for Pará especially. Absence of awareness in relevant areas is a gap.

Q36. What data do you record after each farm visit? Where is it stored — paper, app, central database? — Best practice: digital records with GPS, standardised fields, regular upload to central system.

Q37. Do you record GPS coordinates and farm polygon boundaries for each farmer? Are these linked to their CAR registration? — Critical for EUDR traceability. Absence of geo-referenced farm data is a significant gap.

Q38. How does Kawa use the data you collect? Do you receive feedback or follow-up actions based on your visit reports? — Assess whether data collection drives decisions or is merely compliance paperwork.
Q39. Do you have adequate resources — motorbike/vehicle, smartphone, data connectivity — to do your job effectively? — Resource constraints directly affect quality of monitoring and support.
Q40. What are the biggest challenges you face in carrying out your ESG-related responsibilities? — Open-ended. Look for: time pressure, farmer resistance, inadequate training, language barriers.

Q1. What is your organisation's mandate in the Kawa/IDH cocoa programme? What specific TA activities do you deliver? — Understand scope: agroforestry, certification, gender, traceability, financial literacy, etc.
Q2. How long has your organisation been working in this cocoa value chain and in this geographic area? — Assess institutional knowledge of local context, culture, and regulatory environment.
Q3. How many technical staff are dedicated to this programme? What are their qualifications and languages spoken? — Note: Portuguese and local indigenous languages may be needed in Pará.

Q4. Does your organisation have a formal ESG or safeguarding policy? Is it publicly available? When was it last reviewed? — Ask to see the policy. Absence or outdated policy (>3 years) is a governance gap.

Q5. Are there any conflicts of interest between your organisation's activities and your role as an independent TA provider? — E.g. receiving fees from input suppliers, certification bodies, or buyers you recommend.

Q6. Does your TA programme include specific activities to prevent or remediate child labour? What are they? — Look for: awareness training, school enrolment support, income diversification, referral systems.

Q7. How do your staff identify and respond to suspected child labour during field activities? Is there a documented protocol? How do you engage with Kawa and their field agents in these circumstances? — Best practice: written protocol, trained staff, documented referrals, follow-up records.
Q8. Does your programme track child labour indicators at farmer level as part of M&E? — Quantitative tracking (school attendance rates, incidents reported) is a positive indicator.

Q9. Do your staff receive training on these labour laws, child labour monitoring etc? — Test legal literacy. Training records should be requested. Check for awareness on Brazilian ECA and ILO conventions 138 & 182.

Q10. Does your programme work with local Conselhos Tutelares, CRAS, or social protection services to address child vulnerability? — Integration with government social protection systems strengthens safeguarding outcomes.

Q11. What TA does your organisation provide to help farmers understand and comply with the Forest Code (CAR, Reserva Legal, APP)? — Look for: CAR registration support, RL deficit remediation plans, legal advisory services.

Q12. Are you familiar with the EUDR and its requirements for cocoa supply chain due diligence? Has your programme adapted/ are there still gaps? — EUDR requires geo-referenced farm polygons and post-2020 deforestation-free proof.

Q13. Does your programme support farmers in generating geo-referenced farm boundary data (polygons)? What tools are used? — GPS polygon data is critical for EUDR compliance and deforestation monitoring.

Q14. How does your programme address situations where a farmer's land shows historical deforestation? — Best practice: PRA enrolment support, reforestation planning, transition timeline with conditions.

Q15. Does your programme work in areas with indigenous communities or quilombola territories? How is FPIC applied? — Critical for Pará region. Absence of FPIC protocols with traditional communities = red flag.

Q16. What is your organisation's policy if a farmer is found to have deforested after 2020 (EUDR cut-off)? — Tests alignment with EUDR exclusion requirements and Kawa/IDH deforestation-free commitment.
Q17. Does your TA programme include training on IPM and reduction of hazardous agrochemical use? — Look for: IPM field schools, demonstration plots, alternative product trials, copper reduction.
Q18. Do your field staff check for the use of prohibited or highly hazardous pesticides during farm visits? — Staff should know the MAPA prohibited list. Ask for examples of products flagged.
Q19. Does your programme support safe chemical storage infrastructure or PPE access for smallholder farmers? — Practical support for safety infrastructure is a positive indicator.

Q20. How do you handle situations where a farmer is using a product your programme has identified as high risk? — Listen for: advisory, documentation, referral to Kawa, exclusion criteria application.

Q21. Does your programme work with farmers on soil health, agroforestry, and organic inputs as alternatives to synthetic inputs? — Climate resilience and chemical reduction go hand-in-hand. Positive indicator.

Q22. Does your programme have explicit gender targets or a gender action plan? What % of beneficiaries are women? — Best practice: >40% women beneficiaries, gender-disaggregated data, women in leadership.

Q23. How does your programme reach women farmers who face mobility restrictions, lower literacy, or limited mobile access? — Inclusive design should address specific barriers. Note practical adaptations.
Q24. Does your programme address women's land rights and access to credit? Activities for female-headed households? — Women's tenure security and financial inclusion are core IFC PS 1 indicators.
Q25. Are training materials available in local languages and adapted for low-literacy participants? — In Pará especially, indigenous languages may be needed. Note availability.
Q26. Does your organisation have a PSEAH (protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment) policy? — A PSEAH policy is a minimum standard for any NGO working with vulnerable populations.

Q27. How are the needs of indigenous and quilombola communities specifically addressed in your programme design? — Look for: separate workplans, culturally adapted materials, indigenous staff, FPIC processes.
Q28. What is your programme's M&E framework? What ESG indicators do you track at farmer level? — Should include: child labour incidents, CAR compliance rate, PPE use, women beneficiaries, income.
Q29. How is data collected — paper forms, mobile apps, GPS? How is data quality controlled and verified? — Digital data collection with GPS is the standard. Note any data quality audits.
Q30. How frequently do you report programme data to Kawa? In what format? — Regular, standardised reporting (quarterly minimum) with ESG indicators is expected.
Q31. Has your programme been subject to an independent external evaluation? What were the key findings? — External evaluations test rigour and accountability. Ask for the evaluation report.

Q32. Do you have a system for tracking and responding to grievances raised by beneficiaries? How many in last 12 months? — A functioning grievance log with resolution rates is a key accountability indicator.

Q33. How do you ensure programme data is not influenced by pressure from Kawa or IDH to show positive results? — Tests independence. Listen for: firewall between M&E and programme delivery, independent verification.
SECTION 7 — COORDINATION WITH KAWA & STRATEGIC ALIGNMENT
Q34. How does your organisation coordinate with Kawa's field extension agents on farm visits and technical advice? — Good coordination avoids duplication and ensures consistent farmer messaging.

Q35. Are there areas where your technical advice to farmers has conflicted with Kawa's commercial or operational interests? — Tests independence and whether commercial pressure compromises TA quality.

Q36. Does your programme have any role in recommending or endorsing specific input suppliers, buyers, or financial products? — Conflict of interest if NGO receives commission or benefit from commercial recommendations.

Q37. How do you share ESG risk information — child labour, deforestation, forced labour — with Kawa? Is there a formal protocol? — Information sharing protocol is essential. Ad hoc sharing creates accountability gaps.
Q38. What, in your assessment, are the top three ESG risks in the Kawa cocoa supply chain in this region? — Open-ended. Captures expert field perspective. Note risks not already covered.

Q39. Are there any practices or policies of Kawa you believe are inconsistent with good ESG standards? Have you raised these formally? — Tests whether NGO is a genuine watchdog or merely a service provider.
Q40. What additional support — from Kawa, IDH, or other funders — would most improve ESG outcomes in this supply chain? — Captures unmet needs and systemic gaps from a practitioner perspective.

EXCLUSION TRIGGERS — Escalate immediately: (1) Post-2020 deforestation on farm polygon | (2) Farm overlaps Indigenous Land / quilombola territory / IBAMA embargo | (3) Child labour in worst forms | (4) Forced / bonded labour | (5) WHO Class Ia/Ib or MAPA-prohibited pesticides | (6) Farm inside Federal Conservation Unit
